extracted.intended_audience: scholars, students and researchers in sociology, political science and criminology interested in state theory, policing and political crisis
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and analysing the political, economic and ideological conditions and mechanisms by which a capitalist 'crisis' is signified and managed, producing a shift toward a law-and-order or 'exceptional' state. The focus is on stages (economic, party relations, state, legitimacy) and processes (moral panics, displacement, convergence) that legitimise coercive state measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis of British capitalism (economic base / late-capitalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: "First, it is a crisis of and for British capitalism: the crisis, specifically, of an advanced industrial capitalist nation, seeking to stabilise itself in rapidly changing global and national conditions on an extremely weak, post‑imperial economic base."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterised by an unfinished transition to 'late' capitalism, a weak industrial/economic base, and a short-lived period of affluence; this structural economic weakness is the underlying condition shaping political and social phenomena and should be treated as the first criterion when diagnosing the crisis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis of the relations of social forces / 'Party' (political class struggle)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Second, then, it is a crisis of the 'relations of social forces' engendered by this deep rupture at the economic level - a crisis in the political class struggle and in the political apparatuses... the matter of the crisis of 'Party'..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse changes in organised political interests and alliances (class blocs, parties, labourism). Key indicators include fragmentation or re‑formation of class alliances, the role of Labour as an alternative manager of the crisis, and the incorporation/containment of working‑class institutions into crisis management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis of the state (reconstruction and enlargement of state functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Third, then, it has been a crisis of the state. The entry into 'late capitalism' demands a thorough reconstruction of the capitalist state, an enlargement of its sphere, its apparatuses, its relation to civil society."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the state's expanding direct economic role, corporate-style crisis management on behalf of capital, and new state apparatuses for securing conditions for capital. Examine how conflicts are precipitated onto the terrain of the state and how the state mobilises resources to manage those conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis in political legitimacy, social authority and hegemony (consent vs coercion)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Fourth, it is a crisis in political legitimacy, in social authority, in hegemony, and in the forms of class struggle and resistance... the degree of success in the exercise of hegemony — leadership based on consent, rather than on an excess of force — has to do... with the management of society."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the erosion of consensual hegemony: whether consent is still the principal mode of rule or whether legitimacy is weakening. Look for signs of 'managed dissensus' where consent is grudging and achieved via symbolic/normative work rather than spontaneous legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift from consent to coercion as a diagnostic indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: "The pendulum within the exercise of hegemony tilts; decisively, from that where consent over-rides coercion, to that condition in which coercion becomes, as it were, the natural and routine form in which consent is secured."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track the progressive institutionalisation of coercive measures (surveillance, stop-and-hold, policing tactics, emergency powers) and their normalization. Consider both 'above' (state/elite) and 'below' (popular) levels where coercion gains legitimacy and becomes routine management of conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Birth of a 'law-and-order' society / 'exceptional state' (distinctive form of authoritarianism)
rubrics_metrics.description: "We have called it 'the birth of a law-and-order society'. ... For the first time since the war, of an organised and articulate fraction of the radical right within the leadership... each 'step towards a more authoritarian posture is accompanied by a powerful groundswell of popular legitimacy.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate this 'exceptional' form from overt coups or military dictatorships: the civil power and liberal institutions remain formally intact while authority expands, repressive practices become routine, and popular legitimacy is mobilised for restrictive measures. Examine how state power is exercised under the guise of preserving order and national interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral panic as displacement effect and mechanism for legitimising control
rubrics_metrics.description: "Crucially, in the early years of our period, it is sustained by what we call a displacement effect: the connection between the crisis and the way it is appropriated in the social experience of the majority ... passes through a series of false 'resolutions', primarily taking the shape of a succession of moral panics."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify cycles where social anxieties are channelled into episodic moral panics (youth culture, race, crime, permissiveness). Use evidence of recurrent, short-lived panics that temporarily appease anxiety but ultimately recirculate the issue as an indicator of political manoeuvring to legitimise control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence of moral panics into a 'general conspiracy' (naming and unifying multiple threats)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The second stage is where particular moral panics converge and overlap: where the enemy becomes both many‑faceted and 'one'... This is the point where the crisis appears in its most abstract form: as a 'general conspiracy.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for discourse and policy that link diverse social issues (drugs, pornography, women's movement, immigration, crime) into a single threat narrative. This misleading concreteness (naming 'folk‑devils') legitimises broad, generalized state powers and the temporary suspension of liberties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managed dissensus and the exhaustion of consensus ideologies
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is more akin to what we have characterised as 'managed dissensus' — that undisputed social authority which constitutes 'hegemony' in its proper sense is no longer in place. Consent is won, grudgingly, at the expense only of successive ruptures and breakdowns..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this concept to evaluate whether political leadership relies on continuous ideological labour (manufacturing a 'national interest', episodic consensus) rather than stable hegemonic consent. Indicators: repeated ideological interventions, fragility of appeals to unity, and reliance on short-term moral panics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideology as mis-interpretation and the need to analyse signifying mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: "Ideology is an inflection or misrepresentation of real relations, a displacement of the class struggle... It is of the utmost importance to analyse, precisely, the mechanisms through which the tilt in the crisis of hegemony, from consent to coercion, is publicly signified."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating accounts or policies, examine how ideological frames (media narratives, official rhetoric, moral entrepreneurs) distort structural causes into moral/individual causes. Trace rhetorical devices, symbolic constructions, and institutional actors that convert structural crisis into morally framed threats.
